 CLEVELAND, OHIO – OCTOBER 24: Head coach Jordi Fernandez of the Brooklyn Nets yells to his players during the first quarter against the Cleveland Cavaliers at Rocket Arena on October 24, 2026 in Cleveland, Ohio. (Photo by Jason Miller/Getty Images) 
 By C.J. Holmes | cholmes@nydailynews.com | New York Daily News PUBLISHED: October 25, 2026 at 5:45 PM EDT The play was over. The Nets couldn’t move on.
 Twice in Saturday’s 125-121 loss to the Cleveland Cavaliers , a turnover or a poor shot brought complaining or disappointment that kept players from getting back on defense, head coach Jordi Fernández said. The ball had changed hands. Brooklyn’s attention hadn’t caught up.
 Those are expensive seconds for a team learning how to win together. They also get at the challenge behind Fernández’s early-season patience. Mistakes come with the territory. The Nets have to learn how to leave them behind.
 “You don’t play four quarters of perfect basketball,” Fernández said before Sunday’s game against the Indiana Pacers. “That’s why you have to learn how to accept your mistakes and how to move from them.”
 The loss offered both frustration and possibility. Brooklyn fell behind by 22, then scored 41 points in the fourth quarter and made Cleveland sweat out the finish. With little room left for hesitation, the Nets found a freedom that had been harder to summon earlier.
 Egor Dëmin felt it. Fifteen of his 22 points came in that final quarter, and the second-year guard acknowledged that the feeling of having little left to lose helped him let his shots go.
 Now comes the harder part of that discovery. Brooklyn needs that version of Dëmin while there is still plenty to lose.
 “I think for me it’s going to be key, how can I go with that mindset from the jump, from the start of the game, and not just feeling like I’m free at the end of the game and being able to get those shots out,” Dëmin said.
 Fernández sees reasons to give the group room to figure it out. Comparing the Charlotte opener with Cleveland, he described less anxiety and more focus on playing. Many of Saturday’s mistakes were honest ones made while trying. The effort had improved, even as the execution needed work.
 The next lesson is how quickly players can give themselves another chance to get something right.
 An empty offensive trip still leaves a defender to find, a drive to meet, a teammate who might need help. Carrying disappointment into that work can leave someone else trying to cover two jobs.
 Cleveland scored 46 points in the paint. Fernández identified late positioning in transition and pick-and-roll coverage among the problems, and said players watched the mistakes on film Sunday and took ownership of them.
 The correction has to happen faster on the floor. A defender who reaches the right spot in time can challenge a drive. A late arrival leaves the next teammate scrambling.
 “When you think too much, you’re too slow,” Fernández said.
 A four-point loss invites scrutiny of the finish. Fernández could find opportunities to change it scattered throughout the night, long before the frantic final minutes.
 “I think we can find two possessions in the first quarter and the second and the third,” Fernández said. “And that’s the mindset we want to have, is how to play with the imperfection of the game.”
